clips.title: Terraform explained in 15 mins | Terraform Tutorial for Beginners
clips.why: The chapter on declarative and imperative: the change of thinking this lesson starts with, explained with a simple server example.
look: Imperative means you list the steps; declarative means you describe the end result and the tool finds the steps.
Listen for what happens when you want a different number of servers: you change the number in the file, you do not write "add two".
Compare it with React: you describe the screen, not the DOM changes.
clips.after: Our sizes map works the same way: adding wide is one new line describing the result, and the plan works out that one launch template must be created.

clips.title: Terraform explained in 15 mins | Terraform Tutorial for Beginners
clips.why: Nana's picture of how Terraform works inside: the core reads your configuration and the state, compares them, and providers talk to the real systems.
look: The two inputs to Terraform's core: your configuration (what you want) and the state (what exists now).
The plan is the difference between those two: what must be created, updated or destroyed.
Providers: AWS is one of many. In the lab we use the local provider, which writes files instead.
clips.after: Our infrastructure repo runs the same loop with OpenTofu and the aws provider, so every PR shows a plan that is this difference.

clips.title: Learn Terraform State in 10 Minutes
clips.why: A real manual change made outside Terraform, then a refresh that notices it, then why state can hold secrets and belongs in a remote backend.
look: The manual change: this is drift, the same thing you cause in the lab by deleting a file.
The refresh: Terraform asks the provider what really exists before it compares.
Why state files can contain secrets, and why teams keep them remote instead of on a laptop or in git.
clips.after: Our state lives in the S3 bucket rhinohealth-terraform-state with a lock, never in git, for exactly these reasons.

clips.title: Terraform Basics
clips.why: The plan and apply steps from HashiCorp's own introduction, on a real configuration, so you see the real output once more before the lab.
look: How the plan output lists each resource with a + in front of it.
apply shows the plan again and waits for a yes before it changes anything.
The summary line with the number of resources added, changed and destroyed.
clips.after: In our repo the plan is pasted into the PR and a person types the yes; an agent never does.

practice.q: Which line in a plan should make you stop and read the reason before you type yes?

options.why: A create adds something new. Check it, but nothing that exists is lost.
-/+ destroys the existing VM and its disk and creates a new one. Find the # forces replacement line to see why.
~ keeps the resource and changes one value in place.

practice.q: Finish the filename so each size gets its own file: sandbox-lite.txt, sandbox-full.txt.
practice.hint: Inside for_each, one name gives the map key and the other gives the map value.
practice.why: each.key is lite or full, and each.value is the machine type. The key gives each file a stable name, and the address local_file.template["lite"].

practice.q: Put a safe change to infrastructure in order.
items: Edit the .tf file to describe what should exist
Read the plan, replacements and destroys first
Run tofu apply and type yes
Run tofu plan again and see No changes
practice.why: The plan is the only moment you can stop a mistake, so it comes before apply, and the empty plan afterwards proves the real world now matches the file.

practice.q: Which of these files belongs in git?

options.why: State can hold secrets in plain text, and a copy in git goes stale the moment someone applies. It lives in a locked remote backend.
It pins the exact provider versions and checksums, so everyone gets the same provider. Commit it like package-lock.json.
That is the downloaded provider plugins, like node_modules. tofu init recreates it.

practice.q: lite and full exist. You add wide to the sizes map and wide = 0 to the warm pool. Fill in the plan's last line.
practice.after: to add, 1 to change, 0 to destroy.
practice.hint: Only the new size gets a new file. The warm pool record already exists.
practice.why: The wide file is the only new resource. The warm pool record exists already and only its value changes, which is the 1 to change.

practice.q: Someone deletes a launch template in the AWS console. Nobody touches the code. What will the next tofu plan show?

options.text: No changes, because the code did not change.
options.why: The plan also refreshes against the real world, so a deletion by hand is noticed.

options.text: An error, because the state is now wrong.
options.why: A missing resource is normal drift, not an error. The refresh drops it from the state.

options.text: It plans to create that launch template again.
options.why: The configuration says it should exist, the refresh says it does not, so creating it is the difference.
